issues.legal_issue: The general residual limitation article does not govern an application to file an arbitration agreement when the application is made under arbitration legislation rather than the Code of Civil Procedure.
material_facts: The applicants sought a court order to file a written arbitration agreement and refer their dispute to the named arbitrator.
The appellate court held the application time-barred under the general residual limitation article, calculating time from when the dispute arose.

The Supreme Court held that the article had been interpreted as applying only to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure and that no contrary intention making it applicable to this arbitration application appeared in the arbitration legislation.
issues.conclusion: The application to file the arbitration agreement was not barred by the general residual limitation article.
issues.legal_principle: The general residual limitation article applies to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure for which the schedule provides no limitation period, not to applications under other legislation unless that legislation expressly or by clear intendment provides otherwise. The Court relied on Hansraj Gupta v. Official Liquidators of the Dehradun-Mussoorie Electric Tramway Company Ltd., Sha Mulchand & Company Ltd. (in liquidation) v. Jawahar Mills Ltd., and Bombay Gas Company Ltd. v. Gopal Bhiva.

rule.if: application_to_file_arbitration_agreement and application_made_under_arbitration_law and not application_made_under_civil_procedure_code and not contrary_limitation_intention

predicates.application_to_file_arbitration_agreemen: A party applied to a court to file a written arbitration agreement and refer a dispute to arbitration.
predicates.application_made_under_arbitration_law: The application was made under legislation governing arbitration.
predicates.application_made_under_civil_procedure_c: The application was made under the Code of Civil Procedure.
predicates.contrary_limitation_intention: The governing arbitration law expressly or clearly indicates that the general residual limitation article applies to the application.
predicates.application_not_barred_by_general_residu: The application is not barred by the general residual limitation article.

issues.definition: When a party applies under arbitration law, rather than under the civil procedure code, to file an arbitration agreement, and the arbitration law does not indicate that the general residual limitation article applies, the application is not barred by that article.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation provision governing arbitration does not authorize a court to reject an application to file an arbitration agreement because the underlying claim may be time-barred.
material_facts: The applicants applied to the court to file an arbitration agreement and refer their dispute to arbitration.
The opposing party argued that the application was barred by limitation because the right to apply had arisen earlier.
The Court held that the limitation provision concerning arbitration governs the arbitrator's decision on the dispute, not the court's decision on the application to file the agreement.

The Court stated that, when considering such an application, the court must satisfy itself that a valid and subsisting written agreement exists, that it was executed before any suit was instituted, and that a dispute within the agreement's subject matter and the court's jurisdiction has arisen.
issues.conclusion: The court cannot reject an application to file an arbitration agreement on the ground that the underlying claim is time-barred; that limitation question is for the arbitrator.
issues.legal_principle: The provision applying limitation law to arbitrations concerns the arbitrator's authority to decide the dispute and does not govern an application to a court to file an arbitration agreement and effect a reference. The Court relied on section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, and explained its background by reference to Ramdutt Ramkissentdass v. F. D. Sasson and Company.
